name: Rioja

climate: Tempranillo sits in its sweet spot, so the wines can show the style it is known for.

sheet.place: Rioja is Spain's first DOCa, since 1991. It follows the upper Ebro for about ⟦dist|62 miles|100 km⟧, with Atlantic air in the west and Mediterranean warmth in the east. There are over ⟦area|160,000 acres|66,000 hectares⟧ of vines, on clay-limestone, ferrous clay and alluvial soils.
sheet.rules: Reds: Crianza is 2 years with 1 in oak. Reserva is 3 years with 1 in oak. Gran Reserva is 5 years with 2 in oak and 2 in bottle. Whites and rosados: 6 months in oak at least, then 2 years total for Reserva and 4 for Gran Reserva.

claims.claim: Rioja is a Denominación de Origen Calificada (DOCa), and was the first in Spain. The Consejo Regulador dates the qualified status to 1991 and says its wines have been protected since 1925.

The DOCa has four origin levels: DOCa Rioja, Vino de Zona, Vino de Pueblo and Vino de Viñedo Singular. Vino de Zona names Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa or Rioja Oriental. Vino de Pueblo covers any of the delimited municipalities.
The Consejo set the Viñedo Singular rules in 2017. They entered the official rules in 2018, along with zone and village wines and the name Rioja Oriental, the newer name for Rioja Baja.
The Consejo says Rioja has more than ⟦area|160,000 acres|66,000 hectares⟧ of vineyard in 144 municipalities: 118 in La Rioja, 18 in the Basque Country and 8 in Navarre.

The region follows the upper Ebro valley, which runs west to east near its northern edge, over about ⟦dist|62 miles|100 km⟧ from Haro in the west to Alfaro in the east. Seven tributary valleys cut into the south side.
The Sierra de Cantabria shelters the region from the north. The Demanda and Cameros ranges bound it to the south.

The climate mixes Atlantic and Mediterranean influences. The west leans Atlantic and the east is more Mediterranean, so Rioja Oriental is the warmest and driest zone. Average annual temperature is ⟦temp|54 to 57°F|12 to 14°C⟧ with about 2,000 sunshine hours.
Vineyards climb in steps from the Ebro's river terraces up the slopes, from about ⟦elev|980 feet|300 m⟧. The rules put the top at about ⟦elev|2,300 feet|700 m⟧.

Three main soil types: calcareous (clay-limestone) soils that are yellow-ochre, low in organic matter and rich in calcium; ferrous clay soils that are reddish-brown, deep and compact on the middle hills and higher ground; and alluvial soils that are sandy and stony on flat terraces by the Ebro and its tributaries.
Rioja Alta mixes clay-limestone, ferrous clay and alluvial soils. Rioja Alavesa is mostly clay-limestone. Rioja Oriental is mostly ferrous clay and alluvial.

Haro is at the western end of the region, in Rioja Alta. The Barrio de la Estación is a district of wineries beside the railway station. The Tudela to Bilbao railway reached Haro in 1863, and wineries were built beside the tracks from the 1870s.

Wineries in the Barrio de la Estación include CVNE (1879), Gómez Cruzado (1886), La Rioja Alta (1890), Bodegas Bilbaínas (1901), Muga (cellars moved there in 1970) and Roda (1987). López de Heredia is also in the district.
The usual explanation is that Rioja comes from Río Oja, a small tributary of the Tirón, which joins the Ebro just north of Haro. The name is first recorded in 1099. The origin is not settled.

The main red grapes are Tempranillo, Garnacha, Mazuelo, Graciano and Maturana Tinta. The main whites are Viura, Malvasía and Garnacha Blanca, and several others are allowed. Tempranillo is about 88% of red plantings.
Red Crianza: 2 years total, at least 1 year in oak (225 litre barrels).
Red Reserva: 3 years total, at least 1 year in oak and at least 6 months in bottle.
Red Gran Reserva: 5 years total, at least 2 years in oak and 2 years in bottle.
White and rosado Crianza: at least 18 months in all, with at least 6 in oak.
White and rosado Reserva: 2 years total, with at least 6 months in oak.
White and rosado Gran Reserva: 4 years total, with at least 6 months in oak.
These are minimums. A wine can sit longer in barrel or bottle before release, which López de Heredia is known to do.

terms: Denominación de Origen Calificada, a step above DO for regions with a record of consistent quality. Only Rioja and Priorat hold it.
Young wine, sold with little or no aging. Some see a few months in oak.
In Rioja, a red aged at least two years in barrel and bottle, counted from 1 October of the harvest year.
In Rioja, a red aged at least 36 months, with at least 12 in oak. Whites and rosés need 24 months, with 6 in oak.
In Rioja, a red aged at least five years, with at least two in oak and two in bottle.

notes: Oak aging gives Rioja reds pronounced vanilla flavors, long a trademark of the region, though some modern producers use less oak.
Tempranillo has a fairly neutral profile, so in Rioja it is often blended or aged long in oak, where it takes on the barrel's flavor.

Rioja Alta gives wines with body and high acidity suited to barrel aging, Alavesa slightly higher alcohol and a little less acidity, and Oriental, the warmest and driest zone, riper wines suited to blending.
Some white Rioja Reserva and Gran Reserva ages for decades into a highly distinctive, aromatic wine.

blurb.text: A DOCa, the highest level for a regional appellation in Spain, with vineyards in La Rioja, Navarre and Álava. It has three zones: Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa and Rioja Oriental. Tempranillo is 77 percent of plantings in La Rioja, followed by Garnacha, Macabeo, Graciano and Mazuelo.
